paper_literature_claims.exact_manuscript_context:
BFGS builds its search directions from changes in gradients, yet it often
works well when those gradients jump. Classical convex convergence theory
uses smoothness together with the evolving quasi-Newton matrices
\cite{FND_P76,FND_BN89,FND_N92}. Lewis--Overton's experiments and analyses
\cite{LO} exposed the difficulty of extending that theory: nonsmooth BFGS can
approach a minimizer while its inverse-Hessian approximations become highly
singular. What global or local convergence can ordinary full BFGS guarantee
on convex nonsmooth functions, and how can one prove it without assuming
the asymptotic behavior of its iterates or matrices?

paper_literature_claims.exact_manuscript_context:
Substantial positive theory precedes this work. Guo--Lewis extends Powell's
argument through smooth convex replacements on regions relevant to a BFGS
sequence~\cite[Theorems~3.2, 4.1 and~4.3]{GL18}. The resulting theory proves
Euclidean-norm convergence in arbitrary finite dimension
\cite[Corollary~4.2]{GL18}; for the mixed model
\[
                    F(u,v)=u^2+|v|
\]
Corollary~4.4 gives only a subsequence approaching a point of $v=0$.
The following paragraph explicitly leaves convergence of every BFGS sequence
to $(0,0)$ open~\cite[Corollary~4.4 and following discussion]{GL18}.
Approaching the nonsmooth line does not force the smooth coordinate $u$ to
vanish. Corollary~\ref{art:mixed-benchmark} answers this whole-sequence question
for every admissible full-BFGS run, as a consequence of an arbitrary-dimensional
family theorem rather than a special planar recurrence.

source_comparisons.source_conclusion_or_technique: The manuscript now credits the general extension framework and the norm result, then identifies the specific stronger mixed-benchmark conclusion. It does not describe all Guo–Lewis results as behavior-assumption theorems.

relevant_assumptions.base_conclusion: Objective values approach min f. Additional uniqueness converts value convergence on a compact sublevel to whole-iterate convergence.

For a symmetric $n\times n$ matrix $H$, define
\[
 e_j(H)=\sum_{\substack{I\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}\\|I|=j}}\det H_{I,I},
 \qquad e_{n+1}(H)=0.
\]
These are actual principal determinants. Multilinearity of the determinant
identifies them with the coefficients of $\det(I+zH)$; hence they are invariant
under orthogonal changes of coordinates and equal the elementary symmetric
polynomials of the eigenvalues. In particular $e_1=\tr$ and $e_n=\det$.
Trace and determinant potentials are central to classical BFGS analysis
\cite{FND_N92,FND_BN89}. The determinant records volume, while the intermediate
principal-minor sums retain information about different-dimensional
compressions. The inequality below couples each degree to the next one.
After normalization, this coupling supplies a positive weighted potential
even when the matrices become poorly conditioned.

Suppose the limiting gap is $\ell>0$. On a tail $k\ge J$, use the field
on $K_{\ell/2}$ and ensure $d_k\le\delta_{\ell/2}$; omit the band subscripts.
Set $E_k=\tr(B_kW(x_k))\ge0$. Since
$M_k=\Pi_{s_k}M_k\Pi_{s_k}\succeq0$, trace monotonicity and
\eqref{art:secant-control}--\eqref{art:transport} give
\begin{align*}
 E_{k+1}
 &=\tr(M_kW(x_{k+1}))+
       \frac{y_k^TW(x_{k+1})y_k}{t_k}\\
 &\le(1+Ld_k)\tr(M_kW(x_k))+C
 \le(1+Ld_k)(E_k-m/q_k)+C.
\end{align*}
Trace monotonicity here follows from
$\tr(AQ)=\tr(Q^{1/2}AQ^{1/2})\ge0$ for PSD $A,Q$.
Let $P_J=1$ and $P_{k+1}=P_k(1+Ld_k)$. Summability gives
$1\le P_k\le\exp(L\sum_{j\ge J}d_j)=:\overline P$.
Dividing by $P_{k+1}$, summing and using $E_N\ge0$ yields
\[
 \frac{m}{\overline P}\sum_{k=J}^{N-1}q_k^{-1}
       \le E_J+C(N-J),
\]
contradicting \eqref{art:reciprocal-limits}. This normalization is the usual
summable multiplicative-error argument; compare \cite[Lemmas~2.2--2.3]{FND_CV13}.
Finally, a sequence in compact $K$ with values tending to $F_*$ cannot stay
a positive distance from the closed solution set: a convergent subsequence
would have a nonoptimal limit with value $F_*$. With a unique minimizer the
same argument gives convergence of the entire sequence.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Inward models control radial secants]\label{art:radial-equivalence}

inequalities then give $|F(x)-F(z)|\le G\norm{x-z}$ on $K$.
Use the supporting-plane error
\[
 D_F(z,x)=F(z)-F(x)-\nabla F(x)^T(z-x)\ge0.
\]
This is the usual Bregman expression \cite{BB}; only its supporting endpoint
needs to be differentiable. At differentiable endpoints,
$T=D_F(z,x)+D_F(x,z)$.

\subsection{The specified implementation and the local guarantee at issue}
At a differentiable point $x$, let $g=\nabla F(x)$ and $p=-Hg$.
The line search starts with lower bracket $\ell=0$, upper bracket
$h=+\infty$, and trial length $\alpha=1$. It tests Armijo first and weak
Wolfe second:
\begin{equation}\label{art:failure_tests}
 F(x+\alpha p)\le F(x)+c_1\alpha g^Tp,
 \qquad \nabla F(x+\alpha p)^Tp\ge c_2g^Tp.
\end{equation}
An Armijo rejection sets $h=\alpha$; a Wolfe rejection sets $\ell=\alpha$.
The next length is $(\ell+h)/2$ when $h<\infty$, and $2\ell$ otherwise.
If both tests hold, the length is accepted. This is the unit-first
bracketing implementation of Lewis--Overton~\cite[Algorithm~4.6]{LO}.
All comparisons in the construction are strict, so strict acceptance tests
give the same decisions.

The objective and all starts are chosen before the displayed line-search
parameters. The failure set supplied by the theorem is a sequence of starts;
it is not a positive-measure basin. There is no uniform positive lower
curvature requirement on these branches. Earlier prescribed-orbit
constructions for smooth nonconvex objectives~\cite{NEG_M04,NEG_M07}
suggest the value of designing the dynamics first. Other failures concern
nonconvex objectives~\cite{NEG_LZ15}; see also \preprintcite{NEG_DIAO26}
for a recent smooth nonconvex planar construction. These results do not
supply the convex local claim above. The examples in \preprintcite{NEG_LO08}
use exact search or subgradient choices, and the scaled memoryless failures
of Asl--Overton~\cite{NEG_AO21} concern a different matrix update. Here
the essential combination is convex branch regularity, full BFGS with the
specified search, a common identity initialization, and every query close
to the true minimizer.

paper_literature_claims.exact_manuscript_context:
The specific angular formula has a crucial derivative cancellation:
\begin{equation}\label{art:planar-tangent-cancellation}
 \partial_\theta(hn+h_\theta T)=(h+h_{\theta\theta})T.
\end{equation}
Thus at a smooth point the derivative of $w$ maps the tangent line of a
level curve into that same line. In the orthonormal basis $(T,n)$,
\[
 Dw=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&e\end{pmatrix}
\]
with bounded coefficients. The formula $hn+h_\theta T$ is classical in
normal-angle geometry \cite{geom_Bogosel2023}; see the explicit formula in
\preprintcite[Section~2, equation~(4)]{Bog22}. Here its derivative cancellation
is used for a comparison field, without a convexity requirement on $h$.

paper_literature_claims.exact_manuscript_context:
\emph{The secant correction.}
A finite buffered chart cover supplies a common Lipschitz constant for the
branch gradients. First suppose the endpoints use the same smooth branch
$f$. On a larger convex chart, with Lipschitz constant $L>0$, sufficiently
close buffered endpoints satisfy
\[
 \norm{\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(x)}^2
 \le2L\bigl[f(z)-f(x)-\nabla f(x)^T(z-x)\bigr].
\]
Indeed, subtract the tangent plane at $x$, then use the descent estimate at
$z$ for the step $-(\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(x))/L$. This step stays in the
larger chart for close endpoints, and convexity makes the resulting
function value no smaller than its value at $x$. This proves the displayed
inequality. It is the local convex-gradient estimate underlying
cocoercivity \cite{WW}; compare \preprintcite[Theorem~2.5]{WW22}.
Since the branch values and gradients
at both endpoints agree with those of $F$, the bracket is at most $t$.
Boundedness of $w$ then bounds $(y^Tw(z))^2/t$ uniformly.

paper_literature_claims.exact_manuscript_context:
For completeness, their analytic consequence follows directly.
The centered residual map $N(h)=h-AP(\bar r+h)$ has the exact expansion
\[
 N_i(h)=-(AP(\bar r))_i+
           \sum_{2\le|\nu|\le5}a_{i,\nu}h^\nu;
\]
its linear part vanishes because $AD=I$.
On $\|h\|_\infty,\|k\|_\infty\le r=10^{-30}$, telescoping the
factors of each monomial gives
$|h^\nu-k^\nu|\le|\nu|r\|h-k\|_\infty$, since $r\le1$ and
$|\nu|\ge2$. Hence $N$ has Lipschitz constant at most $7000r$ and
\[
 \|N(h)\|_\infty\le10^{-50}+7000r^2<r.
\]
The closed box is complete, so contraction gives a unique fixed point.
Since $A$ is invertible, this is exactly a root of $P$.
This is the standard preconditioned-residual principle; compare
Rump~\cite[Theorem~13.3]{NEG_RUMP10}.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{art:quadratic_failure}]
The inverse function theorem makes the return map a local diffeomorphism.
The classical local stable-manifold theorem provides a two-dimensional
smooth stable manifold through $P_*$, tangent to the stable eigenspace;
\preprintcite{DY} gives an exposition of this principle and its graph
transform proof. By the last assertion of
Lemma~\ref{art:lower_hyperbolic}, this manifold contains points with
arbitrarily small positive $\tau$.
Choose such a point whose forward return orbit stays in the implementation
neighborhood and tends to $P_*$. Shrinking the neighborhood keeps $r>0$
and $M(b,e)\succ0$, so $\tau^+=\tau r$ preserves positivity. The actual
intermediate matrices remain positive definite by positive curvature.

paper_literature_claims.exact_manuscript_context:
The seed supplied by the stable manifold has a positive-definite initial
matrix $\bar H_0$, common to every copy. Identity initialization is
obtained by changing coordinates once for the whole objective and the
whole sequence of starts, rather than selecting a different objective
for each start. Set $A=\bar H_0^{1/2}$ and $\widetilde F(z)=F(Az)$.
The coordinate identities
\[
 \widetilde g=A^Tg,\qquad \widetilde H=A^{-1}HA^{-T},\qquad
 \widetilde s=A^{-1}s
\]
preserve both scalar line-search tests and
\eqref{art:failure_update}; see also~\cite[Section~2]{LO}.
They give $\widetilde H_0=I$ for this one fixed transformation.
Strong-convexity and smoothness constants become
$\underline\mu=\mu\lambda_{\min}(\bar H_0)$ and
$\overline L=512\lambda_{\max}(\bar H_0)$.
All locality and differentiability statements persist under the
invertible linear map. This proves
Theorem~\ref{art:local-failure-lower}.
